msItem.author: Peter of Cornwall OSA (1140–1221)
msItem.title: Pantheologus (part IV)
msItem.note: Unpr.; Stegmüller Sent. 674; Sharpe, Latin Writers, 425–6; contextual discussion in R. Sharpe and R. Easting, Peter of Cornwall's Book of Revelations (Toronto 2013). This enormous work is in four parts; the entire work is only found in BL MSS Royal 7 E. viii, 7 C. xiii and 7 C. xiv (s. xiiiin, Rochester). A complete copy of part IV is otherwise found only in our manuscript; there are two further partial copies, Oxford, Balliol College, MS 82, and St John’s College, MS 31 (both s. xiiiin). Part IV is dedicated to Godfrey de Lucy (d. 1204), bishop of Winchester, described as a fellow student of Peter’s, which places Godfrey at the London schools under Master Henry of Northampton, the dedicatee of part I. The text includes the Prologus preter rem for Part Four but not the alphabetical headings or accompanying explanatio, suggesting that it or its exemplar may have been the copy for Bishop Godfrey. The books begin at 4v (I), 45v (II), 71r (III), 99v (IV), 116r (V), 134r (VI), 137r (VII), 153v (VIII), 167r (IX), 172r (X), 178v (XI), 225v (XII). 253v (XIII).
Fol. i, a flyleaf of early-modern paper, is blank.
Fol. 257, a flyleaf of medieval parchment, is blank.

Pastedown has some scribbled biblical verses of s. xiv/xv, evidently drawn from memory: ‘qui addit sapientiam addit dolorem, ecclesiastes’ (Eccles. 1:18); ‘in ewangel’ ve vobis qui ridetis quam flebitis’ (Luke 6:25); ‘de risu in die nouissimo prouerb’ 30’ (Prov. 31:25); and another beyond legibility.

supportDesc.support: Parchment. Parchment is well made: smooth and clear, stiff, somewhat cockled at the fore-edge, with little tactile difference between the sides; the pages are clean; the colour is ivory on the flesh-side and yellower on the hair. Arranged like to like, hair-side outermost, except for QQ17–20 which is flesh-side outermost (going with changes of scribe, showing scribal preference). The parchment is very sound, with just a few production flaws: holes or slits in the margins at 8, 49, 60, 62, 65, 79, 81, 90, 104, 106, 110, 114, 117 (stitched), 129, 149, 155, 193, 198, 207, 210, 211, 216, 226, 227, 232, 236, 251; small holes are written around on 15, 35, 36, 45, 64, 68, 92, 96, 104 (an excised bole?), 106, 110, 122 (stitched), 124, 129, 152, 164, 165, 167 (large), 193, 208 (large hole, stitched), 213 (ditto), 217 (ditto), 230; slits and holes stitched before stretching and unpicked at 43, 49, 126, 131, 159, 185 (stitched after scraping, thread present), 201, 226, 244; natural edges at 54 (gelatinized), 95, 124, 127, 178, 193, 199.
supportDesc.foliation: Foliated in early twentieth-century Bodleian pencil, 1–257, including the rear flyleaf in the count but counting 182 twice (subsequently letter ‘a’ and ‘b’).
supportDesc.collation: 1–1810 (fols. 1–180) 1910 (fols. 181–189, foliation counting 182 twice) 20–2510 (190–249) 268 (fols. 250–257). Quire signatures are given by the first scribe from .I. to .VI., centred on the intercolumnar space at the foot of the last verso in a quire. Other scribes preferred to leave catchwords, as on 150v, 180v, 189v, 199v, 209v, 219v, 239v, 249v at the extreme foot at the gutter; vestiges of another at 160v. There are also rough plummet references to ‘qa ii’ (13r), ‘qa iii’ (21r), ‘qa iiii’ (29r), ‘qa v’ (37r), ‘qa vi’ (45r), ‘qa vii’ (53r), ‘qa viii’ (62r), ‘qa ix’ (70r), ‘qa x’ (78r), ‘qa xi’ (86r), ‘qa xvii’ (117r), suggesting that the scribe was working from a similarly sized manuscript made in quires of eight.

layoutDesc.layout: Ruled in lead for two columns of 65 lines, with an intercolumnar space of 12 mm. Bounding rules are single and pass to the edges on both axes; an additional central line is ruled in the middle of the intercolumnar space; horizontal rules cross this central gap and go to the edges at first and second and penultimate and ultimate position. A further vertical column is ruled for chapter numbers in the inner and outer margins, giving a 10 mm space some 5 mm from the written space. Written above top-line. Prickings are sometimes visible in the gutter and occasionally at the fore-edge and also at the foot to guide the vertical rules; otherwise cropped away.

handDesc.handNote: Several English scribes, writing a small, neat, early Gothic hand, with biting and angularity in the bows but not yet laterally compressed. The principal scribe goes apparently to the end of 160v. His hand is consistent, letters are stubby, ascenders short and serifs flat and wide; bows are broken but the aspect is more rotund than angular. Abbreviations are of the common sort, Tironian et is uncrossed. Punctuation by punctus elevatus, punctus interrogativus, and low point. The other hands are very similar, and the number of discernible scribes somewhat impressionistic. Scribe B is at 161ra–168vb l. 18, a more regular and stereotyped performance, narrower and upright. Scribe C is at 168vb l. 19–172vb, smaller, more cursive, like a glossing script. Scribe D is at 171vb–212ra, has more of the black density of the first hand. Scribe E is at 212rb to the end, a thin, squarish aspect; he uses Tironian sign for est and uncrossed Tironian et. Tironian et is crossed for Scribes B, C, D. Ink is mostly black; brown from 156rb to 171va. One rubricator throughout, not obviously one of the text scribes, including for the cross-references to this and other parts of the work, given in the margins; these finish on 78v, which may represent their status in the exemplar. Note that quire arrangement changes, flesh-side uppermost from fol. 170, after a change in scribe.

decoDesc.decoNote: Two large decorated initials at the start of the text, an eleven-line R for the epistolary dedication (1r) and a sixteen-line D for the text proper (4v). Both are of somewhat rustic appearance: the former is of plain red ink parted in reserve, filled with clumsily drawn acanthus scrolls heavily outlined in black against a pale green ground; the latter, seemingly a different hand, is more ambitious, outlined in red with the shaft and arc of the bow filled with pale yellow foliate work, infill of two interlocking acanthus vines of green with red tint and yellow ground, with the same bold outlining. The same hand is behind the initial A at the start of Bk II (46r), a red and green parted initial with the same foliate infill and extension; it is the best drawn of the three. Thereafter, initials for the start of books are enlarged, thirteen-line parted letters done in plain red and green without embellishment: 71v, 99v, 116v, 134r, 137v, 154r, 167r, 172r, 178v, 226r, 253v.

Enlarged initials for new chapters in Bk I are parted initials of green and red with tinted penwork flourishing of foliate style. Thereafter, subsidiary initials for new chapters are less embellished, green or red with line flourishing in the opposing colour; this style itself then becomes only sporadic after 50v, when initials for chapters are routinely plain lombards of three lines, in red and green alternately. This was when the scribe began to leave a larger socket further along the line, allowing the initials to move into the column width rather than stand in their former position in the margin. The artist put chapter numbers in the margins as majuscule roman numerals, mixing green and red for the first book and thereafter red only. He was also responsible for the rubricated running heads, signalling the book, in the form ‘L’ || .II.’ across an opening.

additions.p: Cross-references between the four parts of the work given in the margins peter out after 63r and finish on 78v: these are by the main hand and in the same ink as the rubrication. Two men combined to note biblical references in the margins: the first, not too long after the manuscript was written, noted the name of the biblical book in a small, neat hand, giving up on 11r; the second annotator, of s. xiv2, was the more resolute, adding chapter and verse to the first man’s efforts and then carrying it on through the whole volume. There are otherwise only occasional marks of reading, such as monograms of Nota in various styles, likely to be of the thirteenth-century, and oblique strokes in the margin.

binding.p: By Roger Barnes of Oxford (d. 1631), a binding of the 1620s of reverse calf over pulpboard. Decoration on both boards is restricted to a rectilinear pattern of intersecting lines. Three-line blind fillets to the edges crossing unmitred at the corners, repeated inset at 50 mm to produce a pattern of panels, a rough square at each corner and a central panel, unembellished. Both joints split at the tail and some damage to the headcap, which is torn and pulled away. The medieval sewing structure is retained. Sewn on four double whittawed thongs, raised at the spine. Endbands of undyed thread are non-structural. Two old verdigris marks on the back flyleaf, ranging just left of centre, are signs of pins for fore-edge straps on an earlier binding. In the present binding, paired fore-edge ties of undyed cord are cut away flush to the boards. Fore-edges are sprinkled red. Marks of the early-modern chain-clip are towards the foot of the fore-edge on the lower board, with verdigris on the final leaf. The front pastedown is printer’s waste from the printed edition, found in other Lincoln bindings, of Jakub Schegk, In reliquos naturalium Aristotelis libros commentaria planè philosophica (Basel: Johannes Hervagius, 1550), pp. 482 (upper position) and 491 (lower). The rear pastedown is of medieval parchment and has probably always been with the manuscript, given that it carries medieval scribbles.

provenance.p: Peter of Cornwall was an Augustinian canon of Holy Trinity in London. Surviving copies of this work argue for a limited circulation, given that of the six known witnesses, one was a presentation copy (Merton College, MSS 191–2, to Ralph de Haute rive, archdeacon of Colchester), another may have been, or been derived from, the presentation copy to Godfrey de Lucy (our manuscript), and one other was at Lessness priory in Kent, a house with which Holy Trinity maintained close connections (Oxford, St John’s College, MS 31, of s. xiiiin). All this would therefore argue for production close to or within Peter’s priory of Holy Trinity. There are no signs of medieval provenance in our manuscript.

The other peak of interest in this text was in mid-fifteenth-century Oxford, where the material would have chimed with a then-current taste for large digests of originalia. The Merton manuscripts were given by the sometime warden, John Gygour, in 1486, and a partial copy of part IV, also of the early thirteenth century, was given to Balliol (MS 82), by William Gray, bishop of Ely. Complete sets now lost were in the university library, at Oriel College, and at the intellectually adjacent Syon abbey (respectively, Thomson, Oxford, UO1. 19–20; Bale, Index, 321; Gillespie, Syon, SS1. 682–5). Our manuscript was given to Lincoln College, according to the title-piece, by Thomas Goodall, of Horbury (Yorks), who was a Fellow of Lincoln College from at least 1457 until his death in 1471 (BRUO 777). He is reported as the donor of Duns Scotus on the third book of the Sentences in the 1474 inventory (A1. 128), but this volume is not reported. The manuscript was consulted by Thomas Tanner for his entry on Peter in Bibliotheca Britannico-Hibernica (London, 1748), p. 594, citing the shelf-mark ‘arch. Bor. 29’.

history.provenance: Labels and marks: The medieval title-piece from a earlier binding is now pasted at the foot of fol. 1r: ‘Quarta Pars Pantheologi ex dono | Magistri Thome Goodall’ quondam | socii huius Collegii’ (identifying Thomas Goodall, Fellow of Lincoln from at least 1457 until his death in 1471). Scribally, the label is sui generis, written smaller and more cursively than the usual scripts of these title-pieces. The James number ‘13’ is in ink at the head of fol. 1r. Vestiges of the paper label around the fore-edge near the head of the upper board. In black ink on the fore-edge is the numeral ‘29’. The early-modern press-mark ‘E. 47. 11’ is in the top corner of fol. ir; lower down on the same page is the cursive pencil mark ‘a5’ (or ‘ab’, possibly for ‘arch bor’) and ‘C6’; and at the centre of the page is pencilled the modern Bodleian shelf-mark, ‘MS. Linc. Coll. (c) Lat. 83’. The College bookplate of 1703 is pasted at the centre of the inside front board. On the spine, the usual square paper labels: at the head, the small, square label with a printed numeral 16; in the fourth compartment, the blue-bordered Victorian label with ‘83’ in faint ink, and at the foot, the serrated-edged Bodleian label, mostly rubbed away.
